title: Atomically sharp heteroepitaxial Hf_2C edge contacts enabling barrier-free carrier injection in 2D HfSe_2 semiconducting channels

paper_content.abstract:
Achieving high-quality source/drain contacts in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors remains
challenging due to Fermi-level pinning induced by metal-induced gap states (MIGS). Here, we
demonstrate an atomically sharp Hf C/HfSe edge contact formed via a laterally directed chemical
2 2
conversion, driven by catalyst-assisted hydrodeselenization and carbonization under epitaxial alignment.
Classical and ab initio molecular dynamics elucidate the atomistic mechanism of heteroepitaxial interface
formation. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy measurements confirm suppressed MIGS at
the heteroepitaxial interface, indicating an electronically transparent junction. Electrical measurements
reveal a near-zero Schottky barrier height (≈5 meV) and reduced contact resistance (≈475 Ω·μm) when
compared with previously reported 2D edge-contact systems. When co-integrated with a van der Waals-
integrated native high-κ HfO gate dielectric within a single HfSe channel, the devices exhibit a
2 2
subthreshold swing of 62 mV/dec and on-state current density of 920 μA/μm. This integrated platform
establishes a scalable design framework that couples contact and gate-stack engineering for next-
generation 2D logic technologies.
paper_content.introduction:
As outlined in the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS), two-dimensional (2D)
semiconductors are considered promising channel innovations for sub-1-nm logic nodes1, due to their
intrinsic advantages, particularly in terms of strong immunity to short-channel effects and the potential
for high on-off current ratios2. These merits originate from their atomically thin nature, low dielectric
permittivity, dangling-bond-free surface, moderate density of states, favorable effective mass, and
efficient in-plane thermal dissipation3,4. Translating these intrinsicS advantages into practical device
S
performance, however, requires the formation of high-quality junctions with atomically clean and
E
crystallographically coherent interfaces. In particular, the source/drain contact is critical; achieving low
R
contact resistance (R ) approaching the quantum limit iPs essential for efficient carrier injection and for
C
sustaining high drive current in aggressively scaledN logic technologies5. However, achieving high-quality
contacts in 2D semiconductors remains a long-Istanding and fundamental challenge, primarily due to
E
Fermi-level pinning (FLP) at the metal–2D semiconductor interface, which originates from metal-induced
L
gap states (MIGS). During conventional metal deposition, the metal wavefunction penetrates into the
C
bandgap of the 2D semiconductor, Igenerating interface states localized near the charge-neutrality level
T
and thereby strongly pinning the metal Fermi level6,7. Structural and chemical perturbations introduced
R
during deposition—such aAs chalcogen vacancies, interstitial incorporation, interfacial strain, and metal–
chalcogen reactions—further increase the density of interfacial states8. As a result, the Schottky barrier
height (SBH) becomes largely insensitive to the metal work function, deviating from the ideal Schottky–
Mott limit and severely limiting efficient carrier injection across metal–2D semiconductor junctions9.

To address these limitations, a variety of contact-engineering strategies have been explored, including
doping, van der Waals (vdW) contacts, and semimetal contacts. Doping approaches aim to emulate the
heavily doped source/drain regions in silicon technology, where high doping concentrations narrow the
depletion width and enable direct carrier tunneling into the band edges, thereby facilitating near-ohmic
contact formation. For example, atomic-layer yttrium doping of MoS has been shown to induce a silicide-
2
like metallic phase, yielding an R as low as 69 Ω·μm10. Despite such promising results in tailored systems,
C
the intrinsically high dopant ionization energies and the atomically thin nature of 2D semiconductors
fundamentally limit dopant solubility, generally leading to structural defects and deep-level traps that
degrade contact performance11. Moreover, in 2D semiconductors, the depletion width at the interface
depends only weakly on carrier concentration, making it difficult to realize true ohmic behavior through
tunneling alone. Alternatively, non-disruptive approaches such as charge-transfer doping and interfacial
dipole engineering have also been proposed, enabling localized carrier accumulation via spontaneous
Fermi-level equilibration without introducing structural disorder12. However, these methods are highly
sensitive to ambient conditions and typically require full encapsulation, posing significant challenges for
scalable integration and long-term stability13.

vdW contacts—first demonstrated by Liu et al. using dry-transferred metal electrodes14—offer a
promising pathway to mitigating FLP by physically decoupling the metal–2D semiconductor interface,
thereby minimizing interface disorder and suppressing the formation oSf MIGS. Nevertheless, the inherent
S
tunneling barrier imposed by the vdW gap fundamentally limits carrier injection by reducing the spatial
E
overlap between the metal and 2D semiconductor wavefunctions, even when favorable band alignment is
R
present15. More recently, semimetal contacts have emerPged as a frontier strategy, leveraging their low
density of states near the Fermi level to intrinsically suppress MIGS and mitigate FLP. Shen et al.
N
demonstrated that bismuth (Bi) contact to monolaIyer MoS results in a near-zero SBH and reduced R of
2 C
≈123 Ω·μm, maintaining linear transport bEehavior even at cryogenic temperatures16. Li et al. further
L
advanced this approach by forming oriented antimony (Sb) interfaces, achieving coherent band
C
hybridization across the interface anId R
C
values approaching the quantum limit (≈42 Ω·μm)17. However,
T
such elemental semimetals inherently possess material constraints that hinder their practical use in
R
advanced device integratiAon. Specifically, Bi has a melting point below 300 °C, and Sb exhibits high
atomic diffusivity18, making both incompatible with the stringent thermal budget and reliability
requirements of back-end-of-line processes19. Their propensity for metal diffusion further exacerbates
integration challenges, particularly as diffusion control has become a critical reliability issue in modern
industrial contact integration processes.

Despite remarkable progress in contact engineering for 2D semiconductors, most state-of-the-art
approaches still rely on top-contact geometries. As device dimensions enter the extremely scaled regime,
the contact length (L ) proportionally shrinks, leading to insufficient transfer length (L ) and pronounced
C T
current crowding, which exponentially increases the R 20. Edge-contact architecture has therefore
C
attracted considerable attention, as they enable in-plane carrier injection with nanometer-scale L .
Early
T
demonstrations formed such contacts by plasma etching to expose the 2D semiconductor edge prior to
metal deposition21, validating the conceptual advancement of edge injection but inevitably generating
interfacial disorder that induces FLP and non-ideal Schottky barriers. To mitigate interfacial damage,
subsequent strategies such as epitaxial lateral junctions and thermally induced on-device phase
engineering have been proposed22,23. However, these approaches still suffer from unacceptably high R
C
and inherent limitations in achieving precise, localized stoichiometry, which remain fundamental
bottlenecks to scalable integration. More fundamentally, such approaches are incompatible with the
evolution toward multi-sheet systems, where the physical underlap between the contact and the gated
channel becomes a non-negligible component of the total series resistance3. This parasitic resistance
introduces an additional voltage drop between the contact and the active channel region, lowering the
effective gate overdrive and partially offsetting the gains from R reduction and ultimately constraining
C
overall supply voltage scaling. Hence, establishing and understanding a genuinely laterally directed, high-
quality edge contact to 2D semiconductors is essential for advancing contact engineering beyond the
current limits.

In this work, we present an interface-engineered straPtegy for integrating an atomically sharp-edge-
embedded contact in a 2D semiconductor. By inducing simultaneous edge-initiated hydrodeselenization
and carbonization of HfSe under thermally anId catalytically activated conditions via a controllable
2
chemical vapor deposition (CVD) process—Ethereby converting HfSe into Hf C—an atomically sharp
2 2
L
heteroepitaxial interface was achieved. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations based on
C
density functional theory (DFT)I further elucidated the atomistic mechanism of edge-initiated
T
heteroepitaxial interface formation and the evolution of directionally oriented atomic configurations.
R
Furthermore, we employeAd scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) and Kelvin probe
force microscopy (KPFM) to investigate the local density of states (LDOS) and work function. These
measurements revealed the metallic nature of Hf C with a work function of ≈4 eV, distinct from the
2
semiconducting HfSe . Notably, line STS (LSTS) directly confirmed suppressed MIGS across the
2
heteroepitaxial junction, providing critical insight for heteroepitaxial contact engineering. The high-
quality Hf C/HfSe interface was further demonstrated by the fabricated Hf C/HfSe field-effect
2 2 2 2
transistors (FETs), which exhibited a near-zero SBH (≈5 meV) and a reduced R (≈475 Ω·μm),
C
outperforming previously reported 2D semiconductor-based edge-contact technologies. To further
demonstrate the potential of the proposed edge-contact, FETs with a gate length (L = 200 nm),
g
incorporating a vdW interface-integrated native high-κ dielectric (HfO ) within a single HfSe channel
2 2
were fabricated, exhibiting a nearly ideal subthreshold swing (SS) of 62 mV/dec at room temperature (300
K) along with a high on/off ratio (≈108). The obtained on-state current density (I ) reaches up to 920
on
μA/μm at a drain bias (V ) = 1 V, surpassing the projected IRDS targets. These results underscore the
DS
pivotal role of atomically engineered edge-contacts in achieving low R , representing a major step toward
C
scalable contact engineering and the integration of 2D semiconductor logic architectures beyond silicon.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Bhin et al examine edge contacts for semiconducting 2D HfSe2, via selectively converting semiconductor region to a metallic Hf2C. They conduct STEM imaging, STM mapping, and employ molecular dynamics simulations to understand the Hf2C and HfSe2 interfaces. Lastly, they demonstrate high-performance 2D transistors using these edge contacts and achieve >900 uA/um on-state current. The work is reasonably comprehensive, however there are major points that should be addressed in order to meet the high standards of Nature Communications:
1) The work is quite timely and takes some inspiration from the bismuth oxyselenide work (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41563-025-02117-w) -- obtaining clean high-k and contact interfaces via converting the existing 2D semiconductor. However, the original appeal of 2D transistors is retaining device performance in monolayer semiconducting channels. Because these HfSe2 samples are exfoliated, these are certainly thicker than monolayer and may even have nonuniform thicknesses through the manuscript, which raises several questions:
1a - Can the authors clarify the approximate HfSe2 thickness for all devices throughout the manuscript? This should be inside all of the figure captions and appropriately described throughout the main text + SI discussions. Otherwise, the authors are accidentally comparing monolayer TMD studies to their very thick HfSe2 work, which could be misleading.
1b - Achieving high current densities is an easier task for thick 2D semiconducting channels, even with standard electron-beam evaporated contacts. Is it possible for the authors to demonstrate these contacts on a monolayer HfSe2 semiconductor channel? They have two optional approaches: (1) it appears that the authors can convert HfSe2 to high-quality HfO2. In other words, it looks straight-forward for them to oxidize their already existing devices down to monolayer (or few layer) thick channels and have thicker Hf2C contacts. (2) Reconstruct their edge-contact devices with a fully monolayer HfSe2 to start (e.g., have monolayer contacts too).
1c - It should be clear inside the benchmarking plot which devices are monolayers or few-layers (Fig. 5f). Perhaps a plot with current density as a function of semiconductor channel thickness would be fruitful for the readers to see and contextualize this work's impact also.
1d - HfSe2 has been less studied than MoS2 and WSe2 -- from a theoretical perspective, the band gap is much smaller (1.1 eV bulk rather than 2.1 eV in monolayer MoS2). Is the mobility also smaller? Please cite relevant 2D semiconductor computational work (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41524-024-01417-0). Having this comparison for their devices would be excellent, and again, ideally experimentally measured values for monolayer or few-layer HfSe2.
1e - Si nanosheets have mitigated mobility degradation down to 2-3 nm thicknesses (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10873367). Thus, if monolayer channels are not possible for the authors to fabricate and test, it is important to achieve as close as possible to current Si nanosheet technology thicknesses (ideally below!). Please put some discussion for context -- especially where claiming to meet IRDS targets.
2) Because HfSe2 is a 2D semiconductor that has been less explored all together, it is important that the authors provide adequate control samples using standard top-down contacts. They provide some "Au/HfSe2" data in Supplementary Fig. 18 and Fig. 4a-f, however the inset schematic displays Ti/Au as the source/drain contacts. This is an important point, because Ti or Cr interfacial layers (typically used for adhesion purposes) often lead to high contact resistances across a variety of 2D materials (owing to their high reactivity with O and intermixing, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b01309). If there is a Ti interfacial layer, the Reviewer highly recommends comparing against Au or Ni alone contact schemes, which are more standard for the 2D field for a proper comparison.
3) All contact resistance extractions (both for Hf2C and top-down comparison contacts) should have proper TLM extractions. Although the authors show some TLM data in Figure 4, the extracted contact resistance is not reliable because of exceptionally long channel lengths (3-20 microns long!). Please provide a TLM extraction containing sub-micron long devices - ideally with multiple devices per channel length and thickness for reproducibility - and report those Rc values only. The extraction should be done at a fixed gate overdrive, thus some discussion about threshold voltage extraction is appropriate as well. Output characteristics of short channel devices are also required to strengthen the claim of good contact resistance (both for Hf2C and top-down controls).
4) Please include some hysteresis discussion and plots -- even for the devices without the HfO2 conversion.
5) DFT calculations would strengthen the claim of no in-gap states -- especially for scaled thickness dimension.
Minor points:
6) Please revise for typos and formatting inconsistencies (e.g., μ in SI figures).
7) Having device statistics and a summary table would be good for the reader -- for future works that want to benchmark.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, the authors present a strategy for forming atomically sharp, heteroepitaxial edge contacts to 2D semiconductors via lateral chemical conversion of HfSe2 to metallic Hf2C. The work represents a significant advance in the field of 2D electronics by directly addressing the fundamental challenge of Fermi-level pining. The combination of a novel materials synthesis approach, comprehensive structural/electronic characterization (STEM, STS), electrical measurements, and insightful molecular dynamics simulations is exceptionally strong and compelling. The demonstrated device performance, including a near-ideal subthreshold swing and high on-current, not only surpasses most reported 2D edge-contact systems but also meets critical industry roadmap targets. The methodology and integrated platform established here are likely to have broad implications for future 2D semiconductor technology. However, to fully establish the significance and applicability of this work, the authors need to address several key points regarding the generality, fundamental limits, and practical integration of their technology.
1. The successful conversion is demonstrated on ~40 nm thick HfSe2 flakes. Is this method equally effective and non-destructive for much thinner, monolayer HfSe2, which is crucial for ultimate electrostatic control? For wafer-scale applications, how can the uniformity and control of the lateral conversion process be ensured?
2. The elegance of this technique lies in its potential generality. Beyond HfSe2, is this “hydrochalcogenation + carbonization” strategy applicable to other TMDs like MoS2 or p-type WSe2? Does any preliminary experimental or computational evidence support its generality?
3. The manuscript demonstrates excellent on-state current and contact properties. However, to provide a more complete assessment of the intrinsic channel material quality and the overall device performance, it is essential to quantify the field-effect mobility (μFE). Could the authors please extract and report this key parameter for both the Hf2C/HfSe2 edge-contact FETs and the co-integrated FETs?
4. The contact resistance (RC ~475 Ω·μm) is superior to many 2D edge-contacts but higher than top-tier semimetal top-contacts. Do the authors consider this an inherent trade-off of the edge-contact architecture? What are the strategies for further reducing RC? Furthermore, the RC remains orders above the quantum limit. What are the key factors limiting the intrinsic transport? Are theoretical calculations available to reveal the interface’s transmission coefficient and guide further optimization?
5. In the co-integrated FET, HfO2 is formed by oxidizing part of the HfSe2 channel. Does this introduce a series resistance trade-off? How was this managed during device optimization?
6. Beyond 200 electrical sweeps, what is the interface’s stability under high-temperature operation, high-current stress, or long-term bias? Data from accelerated aging tests would be highly valuable.
7. The manuscript rightly notes the incompatibility of semimetals like Bi and Sb with BEOL due to low melting point or high diffusivity. How does Hf₂C perform in these aspects? Is the Hf2C structure and interface stable upon exposure to typical BEOL thermal budgets? Would it react with interconnect metals or interlayer dielectrics?
8. Finally, to enhance the clarity and professionalism of the manuscript, this reviewer recommends streamlining the reference list by citing the most representative studies. Furthermore, the reference format requires standardization to comply with the journal’s style guide.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, the authors report a lateral chemical-conversion strategy to form embedded Hf₂C/HfSe₂ edge contacts, together with the integration of native HfO₂ gate dielectrics. The work addresses an important challenge in 2D electronics, namely the realization of low-resistance, barrier-free carrier injection without relying on conventional metal deposition. The overall concept is clearly formulated, the experimental implementation is systematic, and the device performance is well characterized.
From a structural and materials perspective, the authors provide convincing evidence for the formation of atomically sharp in-plane heterointerfaces through comprehensive STEM, EDS, Raman, XPS, and simulation analyses. From an electronic standpoint, the STM/STS and KPFM measurements consistently support the claim of suppressed metal-induced gap states and near-zero injection barriers. From a device perspective, the reported contact resistance (~475 Ω·μm), Schottky barrier height (~5 meV), near-ideal subthreshold swing (~62 mV/dec), and high drive current in short-channel devices collectively indicate that the proposed contact and dielectric integration strategy functions as intended.
At the same time, several points would benefit from further clarification to strengthen the rigor and generality of the work:
1. Scalability and process controllability.
The contact formation relies on a spatially selective chemical conversion using masks. While the authors have convincingly demonstrated the feasibility at the flake level, it remains unclear how precisely this process can be controlled over large areas or dense device arrays. A short discussion on lithography compatibility and overlay tolerance would strengthen the manuscript from a manufacturing perspective.
2. Distinction from conventional edge contacts.
Since many recent studies use etched sidewalls followed by metal deposition, the authors should more clearly distinguish “chemically converted embedded edge contacts” from “deposited edge contacts” in the benchmarking discussion to avoid ambiguity in literature comparison.
3. Role of interface dipoles and charge transfer.
The manuscript presents KPFM-derived work function values and a band diagram suggesting nearly zero electron injection barrier. However, the quantitative role of interface dipoles is not fully discussed. It remains unclear whether the observed near-zero barrier is governed primarily by work-function alignment or whether interfacial charge redistribution and dipole formation play a non-negligible role. If possible, an estimate of the interface dipole density or potential step would be helpful.
4. Short-channel transport limits.
Given the very high pulsed current densities, a brief discussion on the dominant current-limiting mechanisms (e.g., velocity saturation, self-heating) would further improve completeness.
5. Device operation at logic-relevant voltages.
Since the reported devices operate at voltages higher than those used in advanced CMOS logic nodes, a brief discussion on possible routes toward voltage scaling (e.g., thinner dielectrics, higher-κ stacks, or reduced channel length) would further enhance the technological relevance of the work.
6. Lin 237-242: Fig 4d presents the temperature-dependent transfer characteristics of Hf₂C/HfSe₂ devices with a long channel length (Lch=3 μm). For such long-channel devices, the Ion is primarily limited by channel resistance; thus, lowering the temperature reduces phonon scattering and enhances Ion. However, when the channel is scaled down to a few hundred nanometers, the current is expected to be dominated by contact-limited current. To clarify this scaling effect, temperature-dependent transfer and output characteristics of shorter-channel devices should be provided.
7. Figure 5 presents the electrical characteristics of Hf2C/HfSe2 devices with a short channel length (Lch = 200 nm). Based on the observed performance, can the channel length be further scaled to sub-50 nm while maintaining functional device behavior? If available, scaling trends or simulations supporting such scalability would be valuable.
8. The HfSe2/HfO2 heterostructure is fabricated through layer-by-layer plasma oxidation. If the terminal HfSe2 layer undergoes incomplete oxidation, could this partial oxidation state introduce oxygen vacancies at the HfSe2/HfO2 interface? Please comment on how oxidation completeness is ensured and whether interfacial oxygen vacancies are detected or controlled.
9. Can the thickness of HfSe2 be further scaled to sub-5nm while maintaining acceptable mobility and gate control? If relevant data or estimates exist, please include them.

We are grateful for this review and appreciate your insightful comments.

Comments:
In this manuscript, the authors present a strategy for forming atomically sharp, heteroepitaxial
edge contacts to 2D semiconductors via lateral chemical conversion of HfSe to metallic Hf C.
2 2
The work represents a significant advance in the field of 2D electronics by directly addressing
the fundamental challenge of Fermi-level pining. The combination of a novel materials
synthesis approach, comprehensive structural/electronic characterization (STEM, STS),
electrical measurements, and insightful molecular dynamics simulations is exceptionally strong
and compelling. The demonstrated device performance, including a near-ideal subthreshold
swing and high on-current, not only surpasses most reported 2D edge-contact systems but also
meets critical industry roadmap targets. The methodology and integrated platform established
here are likely to have broad implications for future 2D semiconductor technology. However,
to fully establish the significance and applicability of this work, the authors need to address
several key points regarding the generality, fundamental limits, and practical integration of
their technology.

 (Approaches for uniform and controllable wafer-scale integration) We acknowledge
the reviewer’s concern regarding the uniformity and controllability required for wafer-
scale implementation of the lateral conversion strategy. Fundamentally, the formation of
Hf C proceeds via an edge-initiated lateral conversion mechanism, rather than surface-
2
wide nucleation. Consequently, the lateral propagation length is governed by deterministic
reaction kinetics and globally controlled process parameters—including temperature, gas
composition, and reaction time—rather than by wafer position or local material variations.
As a result, under identical process conditions, the lateral conversion depth remains
uniform across the wafer. We believe that this edge-confined, kinetics-controlled process
enables reproducible Hf C/HfSe junction formation and provides a physically grounded
2 2
pathway toward uniform and controllable wafer-scale integration. Building on recent
reports of wafer-scale grown HfSe films [R1,2], we plan to investigate uniform and
2
controllable lateral conversion processes at the wafer scale in future studies.

2
 The generality of the hydrochalcogenation + carbonization strategy stems from the
bonding configuration and defect chemistry of TMDs. In layered TMDs, where a
transition-metal plane is sandwiched between two chalcogen planes, the formation of
chalcogen vacancies/defects at exposed edges is a broadly shared feature under thermal or
chemical activation. These chalcogen-deficient edge sites can therefore act as reactive
initiation points for carbon incorporation, enabling edge-initiated chalcogen-to-carbon
replacement and subsequent lateral carbide conversion to proceed in a similar manner
across diverse TMDs. Our previous findings are summarized as follows.
For instance, we previously examined this strategy to MoS , yielding an atomically
2
coherent Mo C/MoS junction, and elucidated the edge-initiated lateral carbonization
2 2
mechanism via reaction-energy profiling and thermodynamic analysis (Figure R1a).
Similarly, we are also extending this strategy to p-type TMDs such as WSe and MoTe .
2 2

 (Edge-contact architecture) We agree that it is important to discuss whether the present
R is fundamentally constrained by the edge-contact geometry, practical routes for further
C
reduction, and the origin of the remaining gap to the quantum limit. At the present stage,
we interpret the measured R as being governed primarily by non-ideal but potentially
C
optimizable factors, most notably non-unity transmission (T < 1) in the injection region,
rather than by an intrinsic geometric trade-off. In principle, an edge contact can approach
very low R when the local mode count in the semiconductor near the injection region is
C
sufficiently high and the interface transmission approaches unity [R1-4]. In our devices,
the extracted SBH is nearly barrierless and the output characteristics remain highly linear,
indicating that thermionic injection over a Schottky barrier is unlikely to be the dominant
limitation; instead, the remaining R is more plausibly governed by the effective
C
transmission and near-interface non-idealities.
 (Considerable origin of the remaining gap to the quantum limit) The quantum limit
corresponds to ballistic injection with unity transmission, and its value depends on the
available number of modes (carrier density) and the transmission coefficient. Importantly,
R extracted from TLM represents an effective contact resistance obtained from a two-
C
terminal resistance decomposition. Within standard planar-contact models, the measured
R can include not only the interfacial term but also current crowding/spreading–related
C
contributions associated with non-uniform current transfer in the vicinity of the junction,
such that the experimentally extracted R can exceed an idealized quantum-limit value
C
even when the interfacial barrier is small [R5]. To further identify the limiting factors that
could reduce the effective transmission, we performed additional first-principle DFT
calculations (Figure R2). It is known that intermixing can happen at the interface, leading
to the formation of C defects in HfSe . To accurately reproduce the experimental band gap,
2
an on-site Coulomb potential (U) of 6 eV was applied to the Hf d orbitals, which yielded
a calculated band gap of approximately 1.07 eV for HfSe . Given that Se atoms are being
2
replaced by C atoms at the interface, we adopted Se-poor conditions for the defect
calculations. Under these conditions, C atoms preferentially substitute for Se atoms. Our
calculations indicate that these substitutions act as acceptor defects, suggesting they are
likely to be negatively charged at the interface. Consequently, if the population of these
charged defects is high, the Fermi level may become pinned at the interface, thereby
hampering efficient charge injections.
 (Approaches for further reduction of R C ) Based on established contact-physics
frameworks [R1-4] and our findings above, we envision several routes to further reduce
R : (i) increasing the local mode count near the injection region (e.g., via local electrostatic
C
doping/contact gating or charge-transfer/dipole engineering), (ii) suppressing interfacial
disorder/defect formation and maintaining interface cleanliness to improve transmission
(e.g., by process optimization and post-processing steps such as rapid thermal annealing
where compatible), (iii) mitigating current crowding by increasing the effective injection
perimeter (e.g., multi-edge/interdigitated layouts), and (iv) further improving the
conductivity of the metallic region to reduce any series contribution in the contact stack.
Furthermore, we acknowledge that calculating the transmission coefficient using the Non-
Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism would provide valuable insights.
However, to accurately model the realistic interface structure, an extremely large supercell
is required. This results in a computational cost that is prohibitively high for the current
study. We hope you understand this constraint.

 We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern that forming HfO 2 by local oxidation of the HfSe 2
channel could introduce an additional series/access resistance if unintended lateral
oxidation encroachment extends into the current injection/access path. Practically, to
mitigate risk of lateral oxidation intrusion during co-integration, the oxidation step is
restricted to a lithographically defined oxidation window that is spatially separated from
the Hf C edge-contact/access region (Figure R3a), while the oxidation exclusion (keep-out)
2
margin is kept minimal so as not to introduce an unnecessarily segment. Cross-sectional
STEM/EDS in the co-integrated device (original Figure 5b; reproduced in Figure R3b)
verifies that oxide formation is confined to the intended gate-stack region without lateral
intrusion toward the contact/access region, consistent with the co-integrated dielectric
formation being unlikely to introduce a dominant series/access resistance penalty in the
optimized devices.
Nevertheless, we acknowledge that a deliberately introduced underlap segment may
appear as a finite access/extension resistance in the channel extension region. However, in
advanced logic integration, underlap/inner-spacer engineering is widely recognized as an
intentional co-optimization knob to reduce gate–S/D parasitic capacitances
(overlap/fringing components) and thereby improve circuit-level RC delay (and intrinsic
gate-delay metrics) [R1]. For example, in GAA nanosheet technologies, inner spacers are
explicitly implemented between the gate and the S/D regions to suppress parasitic
capacitance coupling [R2]. Consistently, device-level studies report that increasing the
spacer/underlap length can reduce fringing/overlap capacitance contributions, leading to a
lower effective gate capacitance [R3]. More generally, the overlap/underlap (or spacer)
dimension is a key geometry parameter that foundries routinely control and optimize to
meet balanced R–C targets at advanced nodes [R4]. In this context, the lithography-
defined underlap in our architecture can be viewed as a controlled, designable feature—
supported by the improved delay results in the original Supplementary Fig. 23b—rather
than an uncontrolled parasitic penalty.

 (Thermal stability & diffusivity) Typical BEOL processing is widely treated as a
≤400 °C thermal-budget regime to protect the interconnect stack [R1]. From an integration
perspective, the primary BEOL concerns for contact materials are (i) thermal/phase
stability and (ii) undesired diffusion. In this regard, Hf–C carbides belong to the
refractory/ultra-high-temperature family; for example, HfC is reported to have a very high
melting point (3890 °C), reflecting strong bonding and high intrinsic thermal stability
[R2,3]. Consistent with this materials trend, SIMS-based studies report minimal Hf
diffusion in Si even after high-temperature anneals, with extracted diffusion coefficients
of (1–3)×10-15 cm2/s at 1000 °C and (3–10)×10-14 cm2/s at 1100 °C [R4], suggesting that
Hf transport is strongly suppressed and unlikely to be limiting under BEOL-relevant
temperatures (≤400 °C). For C atom, C in Si is predominantly substitutional, and the
diffusivity of substitutional carbon under thermal-equilibrium point-defect conditions
follows D = 1.99 exp (–3.1 eV/k T) cm2/s [R5], which extrapolates to the suppressed
S B
diffusivity (≈10-23 cm2/s) at 400 °C, indicating strongly suppressed C atomic transport
under BEOL-relevant temperatures.
 (Interconnect/ILD compatibility) Hf-based layers have been explicitly evaluated in Cu
metallization stacks at temperatures well above BEOL budgets. For instance, ultrathin
ALD HfO films are reported to act as effective diffusion barriers between Cu and Si, with
2
a high failure temperature of ≈750 °C (N anneal, 5 min) [R6]. In addition, Cu/Hf stacks
2
show Cu–Hf compound formation (e.g., CuHf ) after 550 °C annealing, whereas nitrogen
2
incorporation (Hf–N) suppresses Cu–Hf compound formation under the same anneal
condition and improves thermal stability in Cu/Hf–N/Si stacks (depending on N content)
[R7]. From the C–Cu perspective, the Cu–C equilibrium assessment reports no carbide
phases, and measured carbon solubility in solid Cu is very small (4.8–7.4 at. ppm at 1143–
BEOL is also engineered around mandatory barrier/cap schemes to prevent Cu diffusion
and oxidation. Representative dual-damascene flows employ a TaN/Ta barrier to prevent
Cu diffusion into dielectrics [R9] and use SiN/SiCN as an etch-stop (Cu barrier dielectric)
to protect Cu from oxidation and suppress Cu diffusion into low-κ dielectrics [R10]. In the
semiconductor industry, SiCOH (organosilicate) low-κ films are widely used as inter-
metal dielectrics in interconnects [R11]. Within this established BEOL paradigm, potential
reaction pathways between an underlying functional material and the interconnect/ILD are
normally managed by these standard barrier/cap/encapsulation modules rather than by
direct metal–dielectric contact.
 (Summary) The Hf–C carbide family offers a fundamentally larger thermal margin than
low-melting semimetals, and quantified diffusion data indicate strongly suppressed atomic
transport under BEOL-relevant temperatures (≤400 °C). Cu-metallization precedents
further suggest strong diffusion/chemical robustness of Hf-based layers at temperatures
well above typical BEOL budgets, while Cu-C exhibits very low solubility and no carbide
phases in equilibrium assessments. Taken together with standard BEOL barrier/cap
integration modules for Cu/low-κ stacks, we believe these literature-based considerations
support the proposed contact integration as a BEOL-compatible strategy without
introducing dominant thermal or reactivity limitations.

Comments:
In this manuscript, the authors report a lateral chemical-conversion strategy to form embedded
Hf C/HfSe edge contacts, together with the integration of native HfO gate dielectrics. The
2 2 2
work addresses an important challenge in 2D electronics, namely the realization of low-
resistance, barrier-free carrier injection without relying on conventional metal deposition. The
overall concept is clearly formulated, the experimental implementation is systematic, and the
device performance is well characterized. From a structural and materials perspective, the
authors provide convincing evidence for the formation of atomically sharp in-plane
heterointerfaces through comprehensive STEM, EDS, Raman, XPS, and simulation analyses.
From an electronic standpoint, the STM/STS and KPFM measurements consistently support
the claim of suppressed metal-induced gap states and near-zero injection barriers. From a
device perspective, the reported contact resistance (~475 Ω·μm), Schottky barrier height (~5
meV), near-ideal subthreshold swing (~62 mV/dec), and high drive current in short-channel
devices collectively indicate that the proposed contact and dielectric integration strategy
functions as intended. At the same time, several points would benefit from further clarification
to strengthen the rigor and generality of the work:
1. Scalability and process controllability.
The contact formation relies on a spatially selective chemical conversion using masks. While
the authors have convincingly demonstrated the feasibility at the flake level, it remains unclear
how precisely this process can be controlled over large areas or dense device arrays. A short
discussion on lithography compatibility and overlay tolerance would strengthen the manuscript
from a manufacturing perspective.
We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding scalability to large-area implementations
and dense device arrays, including compatibility with standard lithography and practical
overlay tolerance.
 (Process controllability) The spatial selectivity of the proposed contact formation is
fundamentally governed by an edge-initiated, laterally propagating conversion mechanism.
Specifically, the conversion initiates at defined exposed edges and proceeds in-plane,
rather than via a vertical (top-down) reaction through the basal plane. Accordingly, we
consider that the channel interior is inherently less susceptible to unintended conversion,
and selectivity is achieved by defining where conversion is allowed to initiate (i.e., by
lithographically patterning the exposure/edge geometry) rather than by relying solely on
shielding the channel from a vertical reaction. In addition, the converted length/area can
be treated as a process parameter that is tunable by reaction time, enabling a controllable
lateral conversion distance. The reproducible conversion-induced geometric changes
observed in our experiments (e.g., consistent thickness/area changes) further suggest that
predictable processing can be incorporated into layout/design rules for scaled
implementations.
 (Lithography compatibility and overlay tolerance) In our demonstration, a
lithographically patterned masking module (e.g., the SiO hard mask) is used as a standard
2
process-integration aid to define conversion-initiation windows and to maintain
compatibility with conventional patterning/etch/deposition workflows [R1]. Because the
conversion boundary is tied to the lithographically defined edge/exposure geometry and
the conversion front propagates laterally from that pre-defined geometry, we believe the
resulting boundary can be viewed as effectively self-aligned to the patterned features,
which is favorable for dense integration [R2,3]. From an overlay perspective, we consider
that misalignment primarily maps onto conventional design margins—namely (i) ensuring
sufficient overlap between the converted metallic contact region and the subsequently
deposited interconnect metal, and (ii) setting the intended registration between the gate
edge and the contact boundary, as in standard device scaling [R4,5]. Importantly, since the
mechanism does not rely on a vertical conversion through the basal plane, overlay errors
do not translate into uncontrolled conversion of the channel interior; instead, they mainly
appear as a deterministic shift of the intended converted/unconverted boundary (i.e.,
contact extension/underlap) that can be accommodated through standard overlap margins
[R4].
Building on recent reports of wafer-scale HfSe films [R6,7], we will evaluate wafer-scale
2
uniformity and define practical process windows for large-area integration in future work.
From this perspective, we have included a brief discussion in the revised Manuscript as follows:

toward uniform wafer-scale integration can be investigated by coupling it with established

## Abstract

Achieving high-quality source/drain contacts in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors remains
challenging due to Fermi-level pinning induced by metal-induced gap states (MIGS). Here, we
demonstrate an atomically sharp Hf C/HfSe edge contact formed via a laterally directed chemical
2 2
conversion, driven by catalyst-assisted hydrodeselenization and carbonization under epitaxial alignment.
Classical and ab initio molecular dynamics elucidate the atomistic mechanism of heteroepitaxial interface
formation. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy measurements confirm suppressed MIGS at
the heteroepitaxial interface, indicating an electronically transparent junction. Electrical measurements
reveal a near-zero Schottky barrier height (≈5 meV) and reduced contact resistance (≈475 Ω·μm) when
compared with previously reported 2D edge-contact systems. When co-integrated with a van der Waals-
integrated native high-κ HfO gate dielectric within a single HfSe channel, the devices exhibit a
2 2
subthreshold swing of 62 mV/dec and on-state current density of 920 μA/μm. This integrated platform
establishes a scalable design framework that couples contact and gate-stack engineering for next-
generation 2D logic technologies.

---

## Introduction

As outlined in the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS), two-dimensional (2D)
semiconductors are considered promising channel innovations for sub-1-nm logic nodes1, due to their
intrinsic advantages, particularly in terms of strong immunity to short-channel effects and the potential
for high on-off current ratios2. These merits originate from their atomically thin nature, low dielectric
permittivity, dangling-bond-free surface, moderate density of states, favorable effective mass, and
efficient in-plane thermal dissipation3,4. Translating these intrinsicS advantages into practical device
S
performance, however, requires the formation of high-quality junctions with atomically clean and
E
crystallographically coherent interfaces. In particular, the source/drain contact is critical; achieving low
R
contact resistance (R ) approaching the quantum limit iPs essential for efficient carrier injection and for
C
sustaining high drive current in aggressively scaledN logic technologies5. However, achieving high-quality
contacts in 2D semiconductors remains a long-Istanding and fundamental challenge, primarily due to
E
Fermi-level pinning (FLP) at the metal–2D semiconductor interface, which originates from metal-induced
L
gap states (MIGS). During conventional metal deposition, the metal wavefunction penetrates into the
C
bandgap of the 2D semiconductor, Igenerating interface states localized near the charge-neutrality level
T
and thereby strongly pinning the metal Fermi level6,7. Structural and chemical perturbations introduced
R
during deposition—such aAs chalcogen vacancies, interstitial incorporation, interfacial strain, and metal–
chalcogen reactions—further increase the density of interfacial states8. As a result, the Schottky barrier
height (SBH) becomes largely insensitive to the metal work function, deviating from the ideal Schottky–
Mott limit and severely limiting efficient carrier injection across metal–2D semiconductor junctions9.

To address these limitations, a variety of contact-engineering strategies have been explored, including
doping, van der Waals (vdW) contacts, and semimetal contacts. Doping approaches aim to emulate the
heavily doped source/drain regions in silicon technology, where high doping concentrations narrow the
depletion width and enable direct carrier tunneling into the band edges, thereby facilitating near-ohmic
contact formation. For example, atomic-layer yttrium doping of MoS has been shown to induce a silicide-
2
like metallic phase, yielding an R as low as 69 Ω·μm10. Despite such promising results in tailored systems,
C
the intrinsically high dopant ionization energies and the atomically thin nature of 2D semiconductors
fundamentally limit dopant solubility, generally leading to structural defects and deep-level traps that
degrade contact performance11. Moreover, in 2D semiconductors, the depletion width at the interface
depends only weakly on carrier concentration, making it difficult to realize true ohmic behavior through
tunneling alone. Alternatively, non-disruptive approaches such as charge-transfer doping and interfacial
dipole engineering have also been proposed, enabling localized carrier accumulation via spontaneous
Fermi-level equilibration without introducing structural disorder12. However, these methods are highly
sensitive to ambient conditions and typically require full encapsulation, posing significant challenges for
scalable integration and long-term stability13.

vdW contacts—first demonstrated by Liu et al. using dry-transferred metal electrodes14—offer a
promising pathway to mitigating FLP by physically decoupling the metal–2D semiconductor interface,
thereby minimizing interface disorder and suppressing the formation oSf MIGS. Nevertheless, the inherent
S
tunneling barrier imposed by the vdW gap fundamentally limits carrier injection by reducing the spatial
E
overlap between the metal and 2D semiconductor wavefunctions, even when favorable band alignment is
R
present15. More recently, semimetal contacts have emerPged as a frontier strategy, leveraging their low
density of states near the Fermi level to intrinsically suppress MIGS and mitigate FLP. Shen et al.
N
demonstrated that bismuth (Bi) contact to monolaIyer MoS results in a near-zero SBH and reduced R of
2 C
≈123 Ω·μm, maintaining linear transport bEehavior even at cryogenic temperatures16. Li et al. further
L
advanced this approach by forming oriented antimony (Sb) interfaces, achieving coherent band
C
hybridization across the interface anId R
C
values approaching the quantum limit (≈42 Ω·μm)17. However,
T
such elemental semimetals inherently possess material constraints that hinder their practical use in
R
advanced device integratiAon. Specifically, Bi has a melting point below 300 °C, and Sb exhibits high
atomic diffusivity18, making both incompatible with the stringent thermal budget and reliability
requirements of back-end-of-line processes19. Their propensity for metal diffusion further exacerbates
integration challenges, particularly as diffusion control has become a critical reliability issue in modern
industrial contact integration processes.

Despite remarkable progress in contact engineering for 2D semiconductors, most state-of-the-art
approaches still rely on top-contact geometries. As device dimensions enter the extremely scaled regime,
the contact length (L ) proportionally shrinks, leading to insufficient transfer length (L ) and pronounced
C T
current crowding, which exponentially increases the R 20. Edge-contact architecture has therefore
C
attracted considerable attention, as they enable in-plane carrier injection with nanometer-scale L .
Early
T
demonstrations formed such contacts by plasma etching to expose the 2D semiconductor edge prior to
metal deposition21, validating the conceptual advancement of edge injection but inevitably generating
interfacial disorder that induces FLP and non-ideal Schottky barriers. To mitigate interfacial damage,
subsequent strategies such as epitaxial lateral junctions and thermally induced on-device phase
engineering have been proposed22,23. However, these approaches still suffer from unacceptably high R
C
and inherent limitations in achieving precise, localized stoichiometry, which remain fundamental
bottlenecks to scalable integration. More fundamentally, such approaches are incompatible with the
evolution toward multi-sheet systems, where the physical underlap between the contact and the gated
channel becomes a non-negligible component of the total series resistance3. This parasitic resistance
introduces an additional voltage drop between the contact and the active channel region, lowering the
effective gate overdrive and partially offsetting the gains from R reduction and ultimately constraining
C
overall supply voltage scaling. Hence, establishing and understanding a genuinely laterally directed, high-
quality edge contact to 2D semiconductors is essential for advancing contact engineering beyond the
current limits.

In this work, we present an interface-engineered straPtegy for integrating an atomically sharp-edge-
embedded contact in a 2D semiconductor. By inducing simultaneous edge-initiated hydrodeselenization
and carbonization of HfSe under thermally anId catalytically activated conditions via a controllable
2
chemical vapor deposition (CVD) process—Ethereby converting HfSe into Hf C—an atomically sharp
2 2
L
heteroepitaxial interface was achieved. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations based on
C
density functional theory (DFT)I further elucidated the atomistic mechanism of edge-initiated
T
heteroepitaxial interface formation and the evolution of directionally oriented atomic configurations.
R
Furthermore, we employeAd scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) and Kelvin probe
force microscopy (KPFM) to investigate the local density of states (LDOS) and work function. These
measurements revealed the metallic nature of Hf C with a work function of ≈4 eV, distinct from the
2
semiconducting HfSe . Notably, line STS (LSTS) directly confirmed suppressed MIGS across the
2
heteroepitaxial junction, providing critical insight for heteroepitaxial contact engineering. The high-
quality Hf C/HfSe interface was further demonstrated by the fabricated Hf C/HfSe field-effect
2 2 2 2
transistors (FETs), which exhibited a near-zero SBH (≈5 meV) and a reduced R (≈475 Ω·μm),
C
outperforming previously reported 2D semiconductor-based edge-contact technologies. To further
demonstrate the potential of the proposed edge-contact, FETs with a gate length (L = 200 nm),
g
incorporating a vdW interface-integrated native high-κ dielectric (HfO ) within a single HfSe channel
2 2
were fabricated, exhibiting a nearly ideal subthreshold swing (SS) of 62 mV/dec at room temperature (300
K) along with a high on/off ratio (≈108). The obtained on-state current density (I ) reaches up to 920
on
μA/μm at a drain bias (V ) = 1 V, surpassing the projected IRDS targets. These results underscore the
DS
pivotal role of atomically engineered edge-contacts in achieving low R , representing a major step toward
C
scalable contact engineering and the integration of 2D semiconductor logic architectures beyond silicon.

### Reviewer 1

Bhin et al examine edge contacts for semiconducting 2D HfSe2, via selectively converting semiconductor region to a metallic Hf2C. They conduct STEM imaging, STM mapping, and employ molecular dynamics simulations to understand the Hf2C and HfSe2 interfaces. Lastly, they demonstrate high-performance 2D transistors using these edge contacts and achieve >900 uA/um on-state current. The work is reasonably comprehensive, however there are major points that should be addressed in order to meet the high standards of Nature Communications:
1) The work is quite timely and takes some inspiration from the bismuth oxyselenide work (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41563-025-02117-w) -- obtaining clean high-k and contact interfaces via converting the existing 2D semiconductor. However, the original appeal of 2D transistors is retaining device performance in monolayer semiconducting channels. Because these HfSe2 samples are exfoliated, these are certainly thicker than monolayer and may even have nonuniform thicknesses through the manuscript, which raises several questions:
1a - Can the authors clarify the approximate HfSe2 thickness for all devices throughout the manuscript? This should be inside all of the figure captions and appropriately described throughout the main text + SI discussions. Otherwise, the authors are accidentally comparing monolayer TMD studies to their very thick HfSe2 work, which could be misleading.
1b - Achieving high current densities is an easier task for thick 2D semiconducting channels, even with standard electron-beam evaporated contacts. Is it possible for the authors to demonstrate these contacts on a monolayer HfSe2 semiconductor channel? They have two optional approaches: (1) it appears that the authors can convert HfSe2 to high-quality HfO2. In other words, it looks straight-forward for them to oxidize their already existing devices down to monolayer (or few layer) thick channels and have thicker Hf2C contacts. (2) Reconstruct their edge-contact devices with a fully monolayer HfSe2 to start (e.g., have monolayer contacts too).
1c - It should be clear inside the benchmarking plot which devices are monolayers or few-layers (Fig. 5f). Perhaps a plot with current density as a function of semiconductor channel thickness would be fruitful for the readers to see and contextualize this work's impact also.
1d - HfSe2 has been less studied than MoS2 and WSe2 -- from a theoretical perspective, the band gap is much smaller (1.1 eV bulk rather than 2.1 eV in monolayer MoS2). Is the mobility also smaller? Please cite relevant 2D semiconductor computational work (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41524-024-01417-0). Having this comparison for their devices would be excellent, and again, ideally experimentally measured values for monolayer or few-layer HfSe2.
1e - Si nanosheets have mitigated mobility degradation down to 2-3 nm thicknesses (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10873367). Thus, if monolayer channels are not possible for the authors to fabricate and test, it is important to achieve as close as possible to current Si nanosheet technology thicknesses (ideally below!). Please put some discussion for context -- especially where claiming to meet IRDS targets.
2) Because HfSe2 is a 2D semiconductor that has been less explored all together, it is important that the authors provide adequate control samples using standard top-down contacts. They provide some "Au/HfSe2" data in Supplementary Fig. 18 and Fig. 4a-f, however the inset schematic displays Ti/Au as the source/drain contacts. This is an important point, because Ti or Cr interfacial layers (typically used for adhesion purposes) often lead to high contact resistances across a variety of 2D materials (owing to their high reactivity with O and intermixing, https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b01309). If there is a Ti interfacial layer, the Reviewer highly recommends comparing against Au or Ni alone contact schemes, which are more standard for the 2D field for a proper comparison.
3) All contact resistance extractions (both for Hf2C and top-down comparison contacts) should have proper TLM extractions. Although the authors show some TLM data in Figure 4, the extracted contact resistance is not reliable because of exceptionally long channel lengths (3-20 microns long!). Please provide a TLM extraction containing sub-micron long devices - ideally with multiple devices per channel length and thickness for reproducibility - and report those Rc values only. The extraction should be done at a fixed gate overdrive, thus some discussion about threshold voltage extraction is appropriate as well. Output characteristics of short channel devices are also required to strengthen the claim of good contact resistance (both for Hf2C and top-down controls).
4) Please include some hysteresis discussion and plots -- even for the devices without the HfO2 conversion.
5) DFT calculations would strengthen the claim of no in-gap states -- especially for scaled thickness dimension.
Minor points:
6) Please revise for typos and formatting inconsistencies (e.g., μ in SI figures).
7) Having device statistics and a summary table would be good for the reader -- for future works that want to benchmark.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, the authors present a strategy for forming atomically sharp, heteroepitaxial edge contacts to 2D semiconductors via lateral chemical conversion of HfSe2 to metallic Hf2C. The work represents a significant advance in the field of 2D electronics by directly addressing the fundamental challenge of Fermi-level pining. The combination of a novel materials synthesis approach, comprehensive structural/electronic characterization (STEM, STS), electrical measurements, and insightful molecular dynamics simulations is exceptionally strong and compelling. The demonstrated device performance, including a near-ideal subthreshold swing and high on-current, not only surpasses most reported 2D edge-contact systems but also meets critical industry roadmap targets. The methodology and integrated platform established here are likely to have broad implications for future 2D semiconductor technology. However, to fully establish the significance and applicability of this work, the authors need to address several key points regarding the generality, fundamental limits, and practical integration of their technology.
1. The successful conversion is demonstrated on ~40 nm thick HfSe2 flakes. Is this method equally effective and non-destructive for much thinner, monolayer HfSe2, which is crucial for ultimate electrostatic control? For wafer-scale applications, how can the uniformity and control of the lateral conversion process be ensured?
2. The elegance of this technique lies in its potential generality. Beyond HfSe2, is this “hydrochalcogenation + carbonization” strategy applicable to other TMDs like MoS2 or p-type WSe2? Does any preliminary experimental or computational evidence support its generality?
3. The manuscript demonstrates excellent on-state current and contact properties. However, to provide a more complete assessment of the intrinsic channel material quality and the overall device performance, it is essential to quantify the field-effect mobility (μFE). Could the authors please extract and report this key parameter for both the Hf2C/HfSe2 edge-contact FETs and the co-integrated FETs?
4. The contact resistance (RC ~475 Ω·μm) is superior to many 2D edge-contacts but higher than top-tier semimetal top-contacts. Do the authors consider this an inherent trade-off of the edge-contact architecture? What are the strategies for further reducing RC? Furthermore, the RC remains orders above the quantum limit. What are the key factors limiting the intrinsic transport? Are theoretical calculations available to reveal the interface’s transmission coefficient and guide further optimization?
5. In the co-integrated FET, HfO2 is formed by oxidizing part of the HfSe2 channel. Does this introduce a series resistance trade-off? How was this managed during device optimization?
6. Beyond 200 electrical sweeps, what is the interface’s stability under high-temperature operation, high-current stress, or long-term bias? Data from accelerated aging tests would be highly valuable.
7. The manuscript rightly notes the incompatibility of semimetals like Bi and Sb with BEOL due to low melting point or high diffusivity. How does Hf₂C perform in these aspects? Is the Hf2C structure and interface stable upon exposure to typical BEOL thermal budgets? Would it react with interconnect metals or interlayer dielectrics?
8. Finally, to enhance the clarity and professionalism of the manuscript, this reviewer recommends streamlining the reference list by citing the most representative studies. Furthermore, the reference format requires standardization to comply with the journal’s style guide.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript, the authors report a lateral chemical-conversion strategy to form embedded Hf₂C/HfSe₂ edge contacts, together with the integration of native HfO₂ gate dielectrics. The work addresses an important challenge in 2D electronics, namely the realization of low-resistance, barrier-free carrier injection without relying on conventional metal deposition. The overall concept is clearly formulated, the experimental implementation is systematic, and the device performance is well characterized.
From a structural and materials perspective, the authors provide convincing evidence for the formation of atomically sharp in-plane heterointerfaces through comprehensive STEM, EDS, Raman, XPS, and simulation analyses. From an electronic standpoint, the STM/STS and KPFM measurements consistently support the claim of suppressed metal-induced gap states and near-zero injection barriers. From a device perspective, the reported contact resistance (~475 Ω·μm), Schottky barrier height (~5 meV), near-ideal subthreshold swing (~62 mV/dec), and high drive current in short-channel devices collectively indicate that the proposed contact and dielectric integration strategy functions as intended.
At the same time, several points would benefit from further clarification to strengthen the rigor and generality of the work:
1. Scalability and process controllability.
The contact formation relies on a spatially selective chemical conversion using masks. While the authors have convincingly demonstrated the feasibility at the flake level, it remains unclear how precisely this process can be controlled over large areas or dense device arrays. A short discussion on lithography compatibility and overlay tolerance would strengthen the manuscript from a manufacturing perspective.
2. Distinction from conventional edge contacts.
Since many recent studies use etched sidewalls followed by metal deposition, the authors should more clearly distinguish “chemically converted embedded edge contacts” from “deposited edge contacts” in the benchmarking discussion to avoid ambiguity in literature comparison.
3. Role of interface dipoles and charge transfer.
The manuscript presents KPFM-derived work function values and a band diagram suggesting nearly zero electron injection barrier. However, the quantitative role of interface dipoles is not fully discussed. It remains unclear whether the observed near-zero barrier is governed primarily by work-function alignment or whether interfacial charge redistribution and dipole formation play a non-negligible role. If possible, an estimate of the interface dipole density or potential step would be helpful.
4. Short-channel transport limits.
Given the very high pulsed current densities, a brief discussion on the dominant current-limiting mechanisms (e.g., velocity saturation, self-heating) would further improve completeness.
5. Device operation at logic-relevant voltages.
Since the reported devices operate at voltages higher than those used in advanced CMOS logic nodes, a brief discussion on possible routes toward voltage scaling (e.g., thinner dielectrics, higher-κ stacks, or reduced channel length) would further enhance the technological relevance of the work.
6. Lin 237-242: Fig 4d presents the temperature-dependent transfer characteristics of Hf₂C/HfSe₂ devices with a long channel length (Lch=3 μm). For such long-channel devices, the Ion is primarily limited by channel resistance; thus, lowering the temperature reduces phonon scattering and enhances Ion. However, when the channel is scaled down to a few hundred nanometers, the current is expected to be dominated by contact-limited current. To clarify this scaling effect, temperature-dependent transfer and output characteristics of shorter-channel devices should be provided.
7. Figure 5 presents the electrical characteristics of Hf2C/HfSe2 devices with a short channel length (Lch = 200 nm). Based on the observed performance, can the channel length be further scaled to sub-50 nm while maintaining functional device behavior? If available, scaling trends or simulations supporting such scalability would be valuable.
8. The HfSe2/HfO2 heterostructure is fabricated through layer-by-layer plasma oxidation. If the terminal HfSe2 layer undergoes incomplete oxidation, could this partial oxidation state introduce oxygen vacancies at the HfSe2/HfO2 interface? Please comment on how oxidation completeness is ensured and whether interfacial oxygen vacancies are detected or controlled.
9. Can the thickness of HfSe2 be further scaled to sub-5nm while maintaining acceptable mobility and gate control? If relevant data or estimates exist, please include them.

## Paper

## Abstract

Achieving high-quality source/drain contacts in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors remains
challenging due to Fermi-level pinning induced by metal-induced gap states (MIGS). Here, we
demonstrate an atomically sharp Hf C/HfSe edge contact formed via a laterally directed chemical
2 2
conversion, driven by catalyst-assisted hydrodeselenization and carbonization under epitaxial alignment.
Classical and ab initio molecular dynamics elucidate the atomistic mechanism of heteroepitaxial interface
formation. Scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy measurements confirm suppressed MIGS at
the heteroepitaxial interface, indicating an electronically transparent junction. Electrical measurements
reveal a near-zero Schottky barrier height (≈5 meV) and reduced contact resistance (≈475 Ω·μm) when
compared with previously reported 2D edge-contact systems. When co-integrated with a van der Waals-
integrated native high-κ HfO gate dielectric within a single HfSe channel, the devices exhibit a
2 2
subthreshold swing of 62 mV/dec and on-state current density of 920 μA/μm. This integrated platform
establishes a scalable design framework that couples contact and gate-stack engineering for next-
generation 2D logic technologies.

---

## Introduction

As outlined in the International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS), two-dimensional (2D)
semiconductors are considered promising channel innovations for sub-1-nm logic nodes1, due to their
intrinsic advantages, particularly in terms of strong immunity to short-channel effects and the potential
for high on-off current ratios2. These merits originate from their atomically thin nature, low dielectric
permittivity, dangling-bond-free surface, moderate density of states, favorable effective mass, and
efficient in-plane thermal dissipation3,4. Translating these intrinsicS advantages into practical device
S
performance, however, requires the formation of high-quality junctions with atomically clean and
E
crystallographically coherent interfaces. In particular, the source/drain contact is critical; achieving low
R
contact resistance (R ) approaching the quantum limit iPs essential for efficient carrier injection and for
C
sustaining high drive current in aggressively scaledN logic technologies5. However, achieving high-quality
contacts in 2D semiconductors remains a long-Istanding and fundamental challenge, primarily due to
E
Fermi-level pinning (FLP) at the metal–2D semiconductor interface, which originates from metal-induced
L
gap states (MIGS). During conventional metal deposition, the metal wavefunction penetrates into the
C
bandgap of the 2D semiconductor, Igenerating interface states localized near the charge-neutrality level
T
and thereby strongly pinning the metal Fermi level6,7. Structural and chemical perturbations introduced
R
during deposition—such aAs chalcogen vacancies, interstitial incorporation, interfacial strain, and metal–
chalcogen reactions—further increase the density of interfacial states8. As a result, the Schottky barrier
height (SBH) becomes largely insensitive to the metal work function, deviating from the ideal Schottky–
Mott limit and severely limiting efficient carrier injection across metal–2D semiconductor junctions9.

To address these limitations, a variety of contact-engineering strategies have been explored, including
doping, van der Waals (vdW) contacts, and semimetal contacts. Doping approaches aim to emulate the
heavily doped source/drain regions in silicon technology, where high doping concentrations narrow the
depletion width and enable direct carrier tunneling into the band edges, thereby facilitating near-ohmic
contact formation. For example, atomic-layer yttrium doping of MoS has been shown to induce a silicide-
2
like metallic phase, yielding an R as low as 69 Ω·μm10. Despite such promising results in tailored systems,
C
the intrinsically high dopant ionization energies and the atomically thin nature of 2D semiconductors
fundamentally limit dopant solubility, generally leading to structural defects and deep-level traps that
degrade contact performance11. Moreover, in 2D semiconductors, the depletion width at the interface
depends only weakly on carrier concentration, making it difficult to realize true ohmic behavior through
tunneling alone. Alternatively, non-disruptive approaches such as charge-transfer doping and interfacial
dipole engineering have also been proposed, enabling localized carrier accumulation via spontaneous
Fermi-level equilibration without introducing structural disorder12. However, these methods are highly
sensitive to ambient conditions and typically require full encapsulation, posing significant challenges for
scalable integration and long-term stability13.

vdW contacts—first demonstrated by Liu et al. using dry-transferred metal electrodes14—offer a
promising pathway to mitigating FLP by physically decoupling the metal–2D semiconductor interface,
thereby minimizing interface disorder and suppressing the formation oSf MIGS. Nevertheless, the inherent
S
tunneling barrier imposed by the vdW gap fundamentally limits carrier injection by reducing the spatial
E
overlap between the metal and 2D semiconductor wavefunctions, even when favorable band alignment is
R
present15. More recently, semimetal contacts have emerPged as a frontier strategy, leveraging their low
density of states near the Fermi level to intrinsically suppress MIGS and mitigate FLP. Shen et al.
N
demonstrated that bismuth (Bi) contact to monolaIyer MoS results in a near-zero SBH and reduced R of
2 C
≈123 Ω·μm, maintaining linear transport bEehavior even at cryogenic temperatures16. Li et al. further
L
advanced this approach by forming oriented antimony (Sb) interfaces, achieving coherent band
C
hybridization across the interface anId R
C
values approaching the quantum limit (≈42 Ω·μm)17. However,
T
such elemental semimetals inherently possess material constraints that hinder their practical use in
R
advanced device integratiAon. Specifically, Bi has a melting point below 300 °C, and Sb exhibits high
atomic diffusivity18, making both incompatible with the stringent thermal budget and reliability
requirements of back-end-of-line processes19. Their propensity for metal diffusion further exacerbates
integration challenges, particularly as diffusion control has become a critical reliability issue in modern
industrial contact integration processes.

Despite remarkable progress in contact engineering for 2D semiconductors, most state-of-the-art
approaches still rely on top-contact geometries. As device dimensions enter the extremely scaled regime,
the contact length (L ) proportionally shrinks, leading to insufficient transfer length (L ) and pronounced
C T
current crowding, which exponentially increases the R 20. Edge-contact architecture has therefore
C
attracted considerable attention, as they enable in-plane carrier injection with nanometer-scale L .
Early
T
demonstrations formed such contacts by plasma etching to expose the 2D semiconductor edge prior to
metal deposition21, validating the conceptual advancement of edge injection but inevitably generating
interfacial disorder that induces FLP and non-ideal Schottky barriers. To mitigate interfacial damage,
subsequent strategies such as epitaxial lateral junctions and thermally induced on-device phase
engineering have been proposed22,23. However, these approaches still suffer from unacceptably high R
C
and inherent limitations in achieving precise, localized stoichiometry, which remain fundamental
bottlenecks to scalable integration. More fundamentally, such approaches are incompatible with the
evolution toward multi-sheet systems, where the physical underlap between the contact and the gated
channel becomes a non-negligible component of the total series resistance3. This parasitic resistance
introduces an additional voltage drop between the contact and the active channel region, lowering the
effective gate overdrive and partially offsetting the gains from R reduction and ultimately constraining
C
overall supply voltage scaling. Hence, establishing and understanding a genuinely laterally directed, high-
quality edge contact to 2D semiconductors is essential for advancing contact engineering beyond the
current limits.

and carbonization of HfSe under thermally anId catalytically activated conditions via a controllable

2 2

C

heteroepitaxial interface formation and the evolution of directionally oriented atomic configurations.

Furthermore, we employeAd scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy (STM/STS) and Kelvin probe
force microscopy (KPFM) to investigate the local density of states (LDOS) and work function. These
